questions.q: Name the three supporting characters who are physically present during the birth scene in the Morgan household and state one distinguishing trait for each.
questions.a: The three supporting characters are: (1) Joe Morgan — the anxious husband who paces outside, showing strained hope; (2) Mrs. Morgan's mother — the tall, grey-haired grandmother whose "eyes strangely alive and wise" probe Andrew, representing experienced hope; (3) The midwife (Susan) — the stout, elderly nurse who initially places the stillborn child under the bed and pleads "For mercy's sake, Doctor... It's stillborn," embodying traditional resignation. A wrong answer that omits any of these three or confuses the midwife with the grandmother reveals the student cannot distinguish the physically present characters from those only mentioned in Andrew's thoughts.

questions.q: Explain how Joe Morgan's behaviour before and after the birth contrasts with Andrew's internal state at those same moments.
questions.a: Before the birth, Joe paces "with short steps" and says "I know ye'll do well for us" — his outward anxiety and verbal trust contrast with Andrew's inward "queer lethargy of spirit" and muddled thoughts about failed marriages. After the birth, Joe stands "on the pavement with a tense, expectant face" and hears "Both all right" — his relieved certainty mirrors Andrew's newfound clarity ("I've done something real at last"). A wrong answer that only describes Joe's actions without linking them to Andrew's psychological arc shows the student cannot analyse character foil relationships.

questions.q: The grandmother says: "Susan said not to give her the chloroform if it would harm the baby. She's awful set upon this child, Doctor, bach." Apply the concept of dramatic irony to this moment: what does the grandmother know that Andrew does not yet fully grasp?
questions.a: The grandmother knows the depth of collective longing for this child — "Ay, we all are, I fancy" — revealing that the stakes extend beyond medical procedure to twenty years of marital hope. Andrew, preoccupied with his own romantic disillusionment, initially sees only a clinical case. The irony is that the "old woman, wise in experience" understands the emotional weight Andrew has forgotten. A wrong answer that treats this as mere exposition misses the irony: the grandmother's insight diagnoses Andrew's spiritual condition better than he diagnoses the patient.

questions.q: Analyse the midwife's progression from "frightened gesture" placing the child under the bed to "sobbed hysterically... It's come alive." What does this arc reveal about the story's attitude toward tradition versus innovation?
questions.a: The midwife begins as the voice of traditional resignation — she accepts stillbirth as final ("It's stillborn") and follows convention by hiding the body. Her transformation into hysterical joy when Andrew's unorthodox hot-cold immersion works shows tradition yielding to innovative persistence. The text positions her not as incompetent but as limited by experience; her awe ("Dear Father in heaven") validates Andrew's method while honouring the emotional gravity tradition carries. A wrong answer that vilifies the midwife or dismisses her as merely superstitious fails to analyse the nuanced interplay between received wisdom and medical breakthrough.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The supporting characters in 'Birth' exist only to advance Andrew's character arc; they have no interiority of their own." Defend or refute with textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. Each supporting character possesses distinct interiority: Joe's "voice showed signs of strain" and he refuses to enter, protecting himself from potential grief; the grandmother's "meditation had pursued a different course" — she prays silently with "hands together, her lips moved without sound"; the midwife's "stark consternation" and final sob reveal genuine emotional investment. Their interior lives intersect with Andrew's but are not subsumed by it. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim demonstrates inability to recognise round characterisation in minor figures — a senior-secondary analytical skill.

questions.q: Create a 4-line diary entry from the grandmother's perspective on the night of the birth, capturing her voice, fears, and the moment she hears the child's cry. Use textual details to ground it.
questions.a: Sample answer: "Midnight. The doctor looks broken, but I see his hands — steady when they must be. Susan fears the chloroform; I fear the silence. Dawn breaks pale through the blind. Then — a cry, thin and fierce as a new bird. My Susan lives. My grandchild lives. God heard." A poor answer would use modern language, omit the grandmother's distinctive diction ("bach", "ay"), or fail to include her dual anxiety for daughter and grandchild, revealing the student cannot inhabit a supporting character's perspective using textual evidence.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a doctor called to a difficult birth at midnight — the husband paces outside, the ______ watches you like a hawk, and the midwife doubts your methods.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify each supporting character's narrative function, cite textual evidence for their characterisation, explain how they contrast with or illuminate Andrew Manson, and articulate their collective role in advancing the theme of professional awakening versus personal doubt.
